title: Problem 1
statement_text: Does every graph $G$ admit a pivot Gray code on its spanning trees?
context_text: A Gray code on the spanning trees of a graph $G$ is a listing of all its spanning trees in which consecutive trees differ by an edge exchange (removing one edge and adding another): the revolving door property. Cummins showed that such listings always exist; in fact the flip graph (spanning trees, adjacent when they differ by one edge exchange) is edge-Hamiltonian, and this extends to bases of matroids. A pivot Gray code is one with the strong revolving door property: at each step the removed and added edges share a common endpoint; equivalently, it is a Hamiltonian path in the reconfiguration graph of spanning trees under such pivot exchanges. That reconfiguration graph is easily shown to be connected for every $G$, but it is open whether it always has a Hamiltonian path: the usual induction via $G/e$ and $G-e$ fails because uncontracting $e$ does not preserve the strong revolving door property. Pivot Gray codes are known for fan graphs and, more generally, outerplanar graphs. As Knuth noted, a positive answer would follow from his (harder) question whether every directed graph has a Gray code on its arborescences rooted at a given vertex (spanning trees directed away from the root, consecutive ones differing in one arc), by replacing each edge by two opposite arcs. The authors answer Knuth's question positively for tournaments and show that flip graphs of arborescences may have no Hamiltonian cycle.
paper_title: A Gray code for arborescences of tournaments

title: Problem 2 (Knuth)
statement_text: Does every directed graph $G$ admit a pivot Gray code on its arborescences rooted in a given vertex?
context_text: This problem was proposed by Knuth as Exercise 7.2.1.6–102 in The Art of Computer Programming with an estimated difficulty of 46/50. Gray codes on rooted arborescences naturally satisfy the strong revolving door property, so a positive answer would immediately imply a positive answer to Problem 1 on pivot Gray codes for spanning trees of undirected graphs.
paper_contribution: Proves a positive answer for tournaments: for any tournament $G$ and vertex $r$, the flip graph of the arborescences of $G$ rooted in $r$ admits a Hamiltonian path (Theorem 1). Also characterises cases where an arborescence has degree 1 in the flip graph and constructs directed graphs whose flip graph is an unbalanced bipartite graph (hence has no Hamiltonian cycle), showing the general question remains open.
paper_title: A Gray code for arborescences of tournaments
